One exact CTC toy: the helical Misner quotient

This calculator explores a five-dimensional spacetime that is locally flat but globally identified in a way that can make a continuous path close into itself. It is a geometric unit test for A.R.G.O.'s route solver, not a ship or Earth mission trajectory.

What this establishes: a continuous timelike loop is mathematically possible in this quotient. What it does not establish: a historical Earth date, a localized drive, a safe ship trajectory, or photons reaching a witness.

The vertical axis is logarithmic. “Covering frame” means the inertial Minkowski coordinates before quotient identification; this chart has not been matched to an Earth-centered frame.

Acceleration cost versus path duration

For the fixed spatial shift, shortening path time pushes the helical orbit toward a null curve and rapidly raises its required proper acceleration.

Finite-body caution: aℓ/c² is the acceleration-horizon ratio for a uniformly accelerated, fixed-direction Born-rigid rod. This display conservatively treats the full selected span as distance ℓ from its reference point; a center-referenced symmetric hull would use half-span. A value below one only says this local idealization has no Rindler horizon inside that span. The actual route's acceleration direction changes, and this quotient model supplies no hull-support field, internal-stress solution, or collision-clearance calculation. Force per tonne is a required proper-force scale, not a propulsion design.

Model limits: the Misner metric has a compact chronology direction; the helical quotient is global, not a field wall generated around A.R.G.O. Its endpoint is the same manifold event by identification, and T is not an Earth calendar. The displayed speed and γ are measured in the inertial Minkowski covering frame, which has not been matched to Earth. Matching that event to an ancient Earth observer requires a brane embedding and observer worldline; a sighting then needs a future-directed null ray and an optical source. The path requires acceleration: its fixed-T orbit is timelike but not geodesic. No quantum field state or two-point function is calculated here. If this horizon satisfies the compactly generated Cauchy-horizon hypotheses, the standard Hadamard-state extension has a known obstruction at horizon base points; this route animation has not passed that quantum-field consistency check.
